title: Pack a lunch box with the yogurt and the sandwich against the ice pack
instruction: Pack the lunch into the navy box: lay the blue ice pack flat on the box floor, then stand the pink yogurt cup upright and lay the yellow sandwich flat on the box floor, each directly against the ice pack so they stay cold. The red apple and the brown crackers (lying flat) can go anywhere on the box floor.
context: Food-safety guidance for packed lunches (USDA, CDC) is to pack a frozen gel pack and put perishables such as yogurt and sandwiches directly against it; shelf-stable snacks can go anywhere. Perishables packed away from the cold reach the bacterial danger zone, above 4 °C (40 °F), by lunchtime. Done by: childcare workers, school and camp kitchen staff, parents.
setup: An open navy plastic lunch box is fixed to the table midway between the two arm bases (which stand 61 cm apart), its centre 23 cm in front of the arm bases: inside 24 cm front to back and 34 cm side to side, walls 6 cm tall from the table and 1.5 cm thick, a 5 mm floor. Two dark grey rubber mats, 28 cm front to back, 13 cm side to side and 2 mm thick, are fixed 33 cm left and 33 cm right of the centre line, each centred 24 cm in front of the arm bases; every item starts on its mat's centre line. On the right mat: a blue gel ice pack (gel in a plastic pouch, 9 x 6 x 3 cm, 250 g) lying flat, its centre 16 cm in front of the arm bases, its 9 cm side running side to side; and a brown cardboard box of crackers (7 x 5 x 4 cm, 50 g) lying on its largest face, its centre 30 cm in front, its 7 cm side running side to side. On the left mat: a pink sealed plastic yogurt cup (5.5 cm across, 6 cm tall, 150 g) standing upright, its centre 14 cm in front; a red apple (6.5 cm across, 150 g), its centre 23 cm in front; and a yellow wrapped sandwich (a 10 x 6 x 3.5 cm block, 120 g) lying flat, its centre 34 cm in front, its 10 cm side running side to side. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: An item is in the box when its centre is inside the box's inner outline and its lowest point is within 3 mm of the box floor (for the round apple, its centre height minus its 32.5 mm radius, whichever way it has rolled). Lying flat means the item's thinnest dimension is within 10 degrees of vertical (either face up); the yogurt is upright when its axis is within 10 degrees of vertical, opening up. 0.2: the ice pack in the box, lying flat. 0.3 each: the yogurt (in the box, upright) and the sandwich (in the box, lying flat), each only if the ice pack earns its 0.2 and the item's side is at most 5 mm from the ice pack's outline, measured horizontally at the height of the ice pack's centre (its mid-height, 1.5 cm above the box floor when flat): for the yogurt, the distance from the point where the cup's axis crosses that height to the pack's outline, minus 27.5 mm; for the sandwich, the shortest distance between its outline at that height and the pack's. 0.1 each: the apple in the box; the crackers in the box, lying flat. All of it: 1.0. The score is 0 if the yogurt or the sandwich has its centre over the box's outer outline (walls included, at any height) without earning its 0.3: packed more than 5 mm from the ice pack, stacked on or under it, tipped over, packed with the ice pack missing or on edge, or held above the box.
reset_notes: Take the five items out of the box and put them back on their taped outlines on the mats: on the right mat the ice pack flat (nearer) and the crackers on their largest face (farther), long sides running side to side; on the left mat the yogurt upright (nearest), the apple, and the sandwich flat (farthest), long side running side to side. The ice pack need not be frozen for trials; use the same pack every time.
fidelity: Approximate: each item is one rigid shape (the sandwich a block, the yogurt a cylinder, the apple a sphere); nothing deforms, and temperature isn't modelled: a perishable within 5 mm of the flat ice pack stands in for one kept cold. The lunch box and the mats are fixed in place (tape them down for real trials). Every object has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), grippier than plastic, foil or fruit skin.
